reviews.one_line_contribution: When a reflective prompt optimizer (GEPA) is trained on exactly the same episodes that built an ExpeL-style procedural-memory bank, most of the memory-vs-no-memory accuracy gap collapses, and a single frozen instruction compiled offline from the bank (no inference-time retrieval) matches per-instance top-k retrieval at matched token budget — implying that a large share of published procedural-memory gains is really 'gain over an un-optimized baseline prompt' rather than evidence that retrieval-at-inference is doing anything a static prompt couldn't.
reviews.closest_prior_work: MemDelta (arXiv 2606.29914) is correctly identified by the proposal itself as the nearest work: it also shows agent-memory headline gains are baseline artifacts. It threatens novelty on genus (confounded-baseline framing) but not on species (its confound is inside the retrieval pipeline — embeddings, retrieval engineering — while this proposal's is a rival container for the information, instruction optimization, with a compilation prediction MemDelta never makes). More concerning is the proposal's own disclosure: an earlier draft's Preprint Collision Check cited five specific-looking papers (including 'TERMS-Bench,' described by a prior reviewer as 'a GEPA-based substitution test for an architectural intervention in negotiation agents') that the current search could not verify and had to retract. TERMS-Bench, if it exists as described, is structurally closer to this proposal's central move than MemDelta is — using a prompt optimizer as the control for a non-prompt intervention is exactly this paper's methodological trick, just in a different domain. The authors admit they cannot rule this out.
reviews.strongest_objection: Every quantitative claim (S ≥ 0.6 on E1, ≥ 0.7 on E2, the compiled-arm-within-2-points prediction) is carried by a single load-bearing model, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. The only cross-model evidence is an '8B moderation check' restricted to 4 of the 7 grid cells, 1 decoding seed, n=300 — explicitly a risk-factor spot-check, not a replication of the primary claim. The track brief itself flags that a small model 'may fail to follow a long optimized instruction while still using concrete exemplars,' which is precisely the mechanism that would make S model-size-dependent. If substitution strength scales with instruction-following capacity (plausible and not excluded by this design), the actual finding is 'sufficiently capable models can compile their own memory,' a narrower and much less surprising claim than 'procedural memory is a substitutable container' — and a single 14B data point plus a partial 8B check cannot distinguish the two. This is the classic generality objection that sinks single-model empirical claims at ICLR.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Run the full 7-cell E1 grid (not just the reduced moderation cells) on at least one additional model spanning the 7B–32B range the track specifies, so S can be reported as a function of model capability rather than a single point estimate. Separately, restore a minimal (even 2-cell) version of I2 (optimize-with-memory-in-context) — currently cut entirely — since the track's own motivating brief is titled around 'coupling' and lists co-adaptation as open question 4; without any I2 data the proposal cannot speak to whether jointly-adapted memory+optimizer systems (the actual deployed pattern the track describes) behave differently from the independently-optimized I1 arm this study tests.
reviews.missing_baseline: I2 (optimize-with-memory-in-context): the condition where GEPA evolves the instruction while the memory bank is present and retrievable during optimization, i.e. the co-adapted system the track's own abstract describes as the status quo ('agent frameworks now bolt a self-editing memory onto a prompt optimizer'). The proposal explicitly cuts this cell as testing 'co-adaptation, not substitution,' but that means the one deployment configuration practitioners actually use is never measured — the study characterizes independence (I1 built with no memory in context) but says nothing directly about whether joint optimization produces a different, possibly larger or smaller, memory contribution than the isolated-optimizer condition it substitutes for it.
reviews.preprint_collision: Substantive and unusually self-critical: it names MemDelta as the closest work and correctly distinguishes genus (confounded baselines) from species (rival-container substitution, compilation prediction), discusses EvoClinician as a near-miss baseline-table precedent, and explicitly reports a residual risk that OpenReview 2026 submissions weren't swept. But the check also discloses that an earlier version fabricated or could not substantiate five specific citations (ActMem, MAS-PromptBench, TERMS-Bench, MemAPO, 'Evaluating Memory Structure in LLM Agents'), one of which — TERMS-Bench — is hedged as possibly real and would be the single closest structural precedent to this paper's core trick if it exists. A search process that has already produced plausible-sounding phantom citations in this same document cannot be fully trusted to have cleared the field on a second pass; the novelty claim should be treated as provisional, not established, until verified against an independent, human-run literature search rather than the proposal's own retry.

reviews.one_line_contribution: The paper proposes a substitution ratio S measuring how much of an ExpeL-style memory bank's paired accuracy gain over no-memory (cell I0×M1 vs I0×M0) survives once a GEPA-optimized instruction that never saw the bank is substituted in (I1×M1 vs I1×M0), plus a companion claim that a frozen instruction compiled offline from the same bank (cell I0×M2, no retrieval) matches live per-instance retrieval (I0×M1) within 2 points — i.e., that most of what agentic-memory papers currently credit to retrieval is really crediting an unoptimized instruction baseline.
reviews.closest_prior_work: MemDelta (arXiv 2606.29914) is correctly identified by the authors as the nearest published work — it shows agent-memory headline gains (Mem0 vs verbatim RAG on LongMemEval-S) reverse under a controlled embedding-model swap, establishing that memory-vs-no-memory comparisons are confounded. It runs no prompt optimizer and makes no compilation prediction, so it is a genus match (confound-auditing), not a claim match, and I accept the authors' own framing there. More concerning is the self-reported, unresolved TERMS-Bench lead: the Preprint Collision Check states a prior-round reviewer flagged a paper called TERMS-Bench, described as 'a GEPA-based substitution test for an architectural intervention in negotiation agents' — which, if real, is structurally almost exactly this proposal's central move (use a prompt optimizer as the control condition for a non-prompt intervention) — and the authors admit they cannot verify it exists. That is the work that actually threatens novelty here, and it is left open, not closed.
reviews.strongest_objection: The PRECHECK GATE requires the constructed ExpeL-style bank (M1, top-k=7 retrieval — the same design point this research track's own prior controlled evaluation already tested) to clear a ≥10-point paired accuracy gain over no-memory before S is even computed; a bank that fails is 'enriched... until it passes.' But the track's own established prior result, which proposals are told to treat as their starting position, found that injecting a full retrieved bank at this same design point fixed zero items and broke six to seven (p=0.031, p=0.016, replicated across runs) — net harmful, not a ≥10-point gain. If that finding replicates in this study's own from-scratch bank (plausible, given the near-identical setup), the authors will tune/enrich the bank until an artificial positive effect appears before the substitution question is even asked. That means S would be measured only in the regime where memory has already been made to work, not in the regime this track's own data shows is typical — so a headline 'S ≥ 0.6' would license the claim 'instruction optimization substitutes for memory' only for hand-picked, gate-passing banks, a materially narrower claim than the abstract advertises. A track-savvy reviewer would ask why the harmful/near-zero-gain regime — the modal case in this track's own prior data — is excluded from the central comparison by construction (via the gate) instead of being reported as a first-class outcome in its own right.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Report the pre-enrichment bank's gain, with its fix/break decomposition, as a headline number in its own right rather than only as a pass/fail gate, and pre-register how much enrichment was required to pass — that quantity speaks directly to how representative the 'memory already works' precondition is relative to the harmful/near-zero regime this track has already documented. Reinstate a reduced I2 (instruction optimized with memory in context, even 1-2 seeds) so the study says something about coupling/co-adaptation, since cutting the one condition that tests actual coupling is the most reviewer-visible gap for a track framed around coupling memory with optimization. Resolve the TERMS-Bench question explicitly — confirm it doesn't exist, or state what changes in the novelty claim if it does — before relying on the collision check as established.
reviews.missing_baseline: I2 — the optimize-with-memory-in-context / co-adaptation arm — which the authors explicitly cut ('it tests co-adaptation, not substitution, and does not carry the claim'). This research track is specifically about coupling self-editing memory with prompt optimization, including whether the pair overfits to each other under joint evolution and where the two fail on disjoint slices; a reviewer for this track would demand at least a minimal I2 so the paper can say something about the coupled condition, not only about the two components measured in isolation and then subtracted from one another.
reviews.preprint_collision: The check is unusually careful for this format: it names specific papers with arXiv IDs, quotes them, explicitly distinguishes 'genus' collision (MemDelta's general 'memory baselines are confounded' thesis) from 'claim' collision, and notably walks back five citations from an earlier draft (ActMem, MAS-PromptBench, TERMS-Bench, MemAPO, 'Evaluating Memory Structure in LLM Agents') that a re-run search could not verify, stating plainly it will not rely on them for novelty. That self-correction is a genuine sign of process rigor, not a weakness by itself. But it leaves a live, self-identified, unresolved threat: TERMS-Bench, described by a prior-round reviewer as 'a GEPA-based substitution test for an architectural intervention in negotiation agents,' is exactly the kind of paper that would gut this proposal's novelty if it exists, and the authors state outright they cannot confirm or deny it. An unverifiable 'closest structural precedent' the authors themselves cannot rule out is not a neutral disclosure — it is an open novelty risk the check surfaces but does not close. The check also admits it could not sweep OpenReview 2026 submissions, where a combined-system paper could contain exactly this ablation in an appendix without surfacing in an arXiv search.

reviews.one_line_contribution: It tests whether procedural agentic-memory's measured gain over a hand-written prompt survives once the comparison instruction is itself optimized (GEPA) on the exact same training episodes that built the memory bank, and separately predicts that a frozen, once-compiled instruction with no retrieval at inference (arm C / I0×M2) can match per-instance top-k retrieval (I0×M1) at matched injected tokens.
reviews.closest_prior_work: MemDelta (arXiv 2606.29914) is the real threat: it already establishes that agent-memory headline gains are artifacts of uncontrolled baselines (Mem0's 72.7-vs-61.4 win over verbatim RAG flips to a 1.2-point loss under a matched embedding model), which is the same genus of claim as this proposal's framing. It stops short of the specific mechanism, though: it never proposes a prompt optimizer as the rival container, never equalizes training episodes across containers, and never predicts that retrieval can be deleted in favor of a frozen compiled instruction. That last piece — prediction 3, the compiled-static-arm parity claim — is the part with no real precedent in the cited literature and is where this proposal's actual novelty lives; the broader 'memory-vs-optimized-instruction' framing itself is closer to prior art, since the track brief's own preamble already flags that combined memory+optimizer papers exist and fail to isolate components.
reviews.strongest_objection: Both headline predictions are load-bearing on a single model, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and the only cross-scale check (Llama-3.1-8B 'moderation') covers just 4 of the 7 E1 grid cells (1,2,5,6) with no positive control (B-dup) and no M2/compiled arm at 8B. That means prediction 3 — the riskier, more consequential claim that a frozen compiled instruction can replace retrieval entirely — is never tested at any scale other than the one load-bearing model. If Qwen-14B's GEPA-optimized instructions happen to absorb bank content unusually well (a property that could be an artifact of this specific model/scale rather than a general fact about instruction optimization), the paper's central practical recommendation ('compile once, delete retrieval') would not transfer to the 7B or 32B models the track's own resource brief says practitioners actually run, and a reviewer would withhold acceptance pending at least one more full-grid model.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Run the full 7-cell E1 grid plus the B-dup positive control on at least one additional open-weight scale (e.g., 7B and/or 32B, both already in the track's stated 7B-32B range) rather than a 4-cell moderation subset, so S and the compiled-instruction parity claim are each independently tested at more than one model scale before being reported as general findings. Separately, pre-register or otherwise bound the bank-enrichment stopping rule in the precheck gate: as written, a bank that fails the +10pt gate gets iteratively enriched until it passes, which risks selecting specifically for the kind of 'instruction-shaped' memory gains GEPA is best at reabsorbing, mechanically inflating S independent of the true phenomenon.
reviews.missing_baseline: A fine-tuning/LoRA arm on the same training split. The proposal's own Related Work explicitly frames memory, instruction, and fine-tuning as the field's three candidate 'containers' for training-episode information (noting ExpeL-class papers are sometimes evaluated 'against fine-tuning'), yet the 7-cell grid tests only two of those three containers (instruction I1 vs. memory M1/M2/M3). A LoRA-tuned arm on Qwen2.5-14B trained on the identical episodes is feasible within the stated 4xA100 / open-weight-model scope and is the baseline a reviewer would demand to complete the container argument — without it the paper can only claim instruction optimization substitutes for memory, not that it is the best or cheapest substitute among the containers the field actually uses.
reviews.preprint_collision: The check is unusually rigorous and self-correcting: it explicitly retracts five citations from an earlier draft it says it 'cannot verify' (ActMem 2603.00026, MAS-PromptBench 2606.23664, TERMS-Bench 2605.13909, MemAPO 2603.21520, 'Evaluating Memory Structure in LLM Agents' 2602.11243) and refuses to lean on them for novelty — good hygiene, and better than most proposals' collision checks. But that retraction is itself a yellow flag, since it means a prior version of the novelty claim rested partly on citations that may not exist, and the current text still spends a paragraph hypothesizing about what would follow 'if TERMS-Bench exists as described,' i.e. partially re-admitting an unverified pointer into the argument. The one collision it verifies and stands behind, MemDelta (arXiv 2606.29914), is real on genus (confounded memory baselines) but not on the specific claim (rival-container substitution plus compile-don't-retrieve), so on the paper's own honestly-reported evidence there is no confirmed scooping preprint — but the check also admits it 'could not sweep OpenReview 2026 submissions,' so novelty here is asserted and reasonably supported, not fully established.
